newsitem.title: JAPAN: Peru is crisis debut for Japan PM Hashimoto.
newsitem.headline: Peru is crisis debut for Japan PM Hashimoto.

text.p: For Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, Japan's hostage crisis in Peru is a chance to show a sceptical world that Tokyo can be tough on terrorism and convince Japanese that politicians can take charge in a country long run by bureaucrats.
The seizure of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru is the crisis management debut for Hashimoto, who as trade minister won plaudits for toughness in car trade talks with the United States.

Successor to an ineffectual Socialist prime minister, Hashimoto took office a year ago under pressure to restore credibility to a government caught unprepared by such 1995 crises as the Kobe earthquake and the deadly gassing of Tokyo subways.

Although mainly a bystander in a showdown between the Peru government and the leftist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), Hashimoto's hands-on approach has won plaudits in a Japan not accustomed to seeing its leaders take command.

Hashimoto has also laboured to shake off perceptions that Japan would use its chequebook to buy the freedom of hundreds of hostages, a move which would undercut the commitment to fight terrorism Tokyo made at the Group of Seven summit this year.

After the kidnapping in August of a top Japanese business executive in the Mexican border town of Tijuana, it was widely believed that the victim's employer Sanyo Electric paid a $2 million ransom to secure his release.

In the five days since MRTA guerrillas seized nearly 500 hostages at the ambassador's residence during a party, Hashimoto has given the crisis his full-time attention, making twice daily visits to the foreign ministry's crisis task force.
A stern-faced Hashimoto one night delivered 130 pastry snacks to officials in the ministry's crisis room, personally unloading boxes as television cameras rolled.

At another point, the prime minister angrily snapped at a reporter who asked questions about the state budget and ordinary year-end political issues, protesting that the fate of the hostages was the only thing on his mind.
The intense round of activity was not merely political posturing by Hashimoto and produced symbolic and practical results, analysts said.

The prime minister's decision to send Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda "should be evaluated highly as a sign that politicians are taking direct responsibility for a difficult problem," said international security analyst Atsuyuki Sasa.
Japan's previous international crises were dealt with by career bureaucrats, he said.

Ikeda spent four days in Lima conducting crisis diplomacy before flying home on Sunday apparently empty-handed and sidelined. However, Ikeda's two meetings with Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori closed the gap between Lima and Tokyo over how to deal with the crisis, foreign ministry officials said.

Ikeda endorsed Fujimori's stern call to the guerrillas to lay down their weapons and release the hostages to avoid bloodshed, shifting Tokyo's attitude from initial softness closer to Lima's hard line.
Japan's insistence on the safety of hostages -- which included top Peru government officials, Japanese businessmen and many countries' diplomats -- has paid off so far, one analyst said.
"The important thing is that bloodshed has been avoided so far," said Kazuhisa Ogawa, international politics analyst.
"Hashimoto's decision to send Ikeda to convey to President Alberto Fujimori Japan's stance (on avoiding bloodshed) has been instrumental in getting the message across," he said.
But with the world watching, Hashimoto "has been given some tough homework," said a Japanese daily.

"It remains to been whether Japan can change its international image by demonstrating to the world it can take a tough stance on terrorism and solve the crisis without loss of life," the daily Mainichi Shimbun said in a commentary.
